reading.body:
AutoGPT alone accounts for 187,019 of the 331,931 stars across these four repositories, meaning more than half the measured community interest in open-source autonomous agents concentrates in a single project.

The remaining three repositories divide the rest unevenly. OpenHands holds 85,699 stars and remains actively maintained. gpt-engineer, with 55,113 stars, is archived and its own description marks it as a precursor to a commercial product, so its star count reflects historical interest rather than current development activity. Langroid, at 4,100 stars, is the only project explicitly framed around multi-agent rather than single-agent design. The gap between the top two projects and the bottom two is large enough that this is not a flat field of competing alternatives.

Three of the four licences are MIT, meaning the code is freely reusable. The fourth, AutoGPT, carries a custom licence whose terms this data does not specify, which matters for anyone planning to build on it. What the data does not cover is runtime behavior: how much compute these agents consume per task, how that consumption scales with task complexity, or what infrastructure is required to run them at production load. The star counts measure developer attention, not deployment scale, and the two are not the same thing.
